newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF says has no intention to sell U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: MOF says has no intention to sell U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters on Tuesday that Japan has not sold U.S. Treasuries and has no intention of doing so.
He did not specify any time frame.
"We have not tried to sell U.S. Treasuries and the ministry has not thought about it," he said.
"We have no such intention at present," he said.

Close cooperation between Japan and the United States for currency stability is of the utmost importance and the two nations have been in close contact (on the issue), which is important for stability, he said.
Mitsuzuka also said he welcomed efforts made by U.S. authorities, including Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, in seeking stability in exchange rates.

Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech at Columbia University in New York on Monday, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.

"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," Hashimoto added.

The remark undermined the dollar in New York and ignited a sell-off in U.S. shares which sliced 192.25 points off the Dow Jones industrial average, a point decline second only to the 508-point drop when the market crashed on October 19, 1987.
Hashimoto's comments on Japanese investments in U.S. Treasuries were incorrectly reported, Mitsuzuka added.
"The prime minister's real intention was not reported correctly," he said, without elaborating.
